No, that's not right, and it matters for your design. A language model doesn't remember earlier conversations on its own.

Each time you call a model, it sees only the text you send in that call. It keeps nothing between calls. A chatbot seems to remember because the app resends the earlier messages with every new one. Close the chat and start a new one, and the model has no trace of the old one.

Here is what that means for your makerspace assistant. A student tells it on Monday, "I finished the laser cutter training." On Friday they start a new session. The model sees only Friday's message, so it has no idea about Monday.

To make it remember, your code has to do three things:
1. Save the fact somewhere durable, such as a database row or a JSON file (you already know both from Python).
2. Load it when the student comes back.
3. Put it into the text sent to the model.

The model can only use what you put in front of it. Those saved facts also take up space in the context window, and you pay for them on every call. So deciding what to save and what to load is a budget decision as well as a memory one.

This is the context-and-memory topic that comes next in your mission, so I can turn it into a lesson.

Quick check that this landed: a student says "book me the 3D printer, same as last time." Where does "last time" have to come from?
